pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 💻 **Strand 1 — Introduction To Computing**
Sub-strand 3: Health and Safety in the Use of ICT Tools

In this final health and safety unit you will evaluate ergonomic equipment, good lighting and ways of controlling the heat produced by computers and printers.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B9.1.3.1** Demonstrate how to apply health and safety measures in the use of ICT tools.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B9.1.3.1.1** Evaluate health issues at workstations.
- **B9.1.3.1.2** Evaluate safety risk reduction issues at workstations.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 3.1 Ergonomic Tools and Lighting
- 3.2 Reducing Heat at Workstations

**Core competencies developed:** Communication and Collaboration (CC8.1).

pages.title: Ergonomic Tools and Lighting
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.1.3.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- discuss ergonomic tools;
- demonstrate appropriate lighting for computer work.
| **Ergonomic tool** | **How it helps** |
|---|---|
| Ergonomic keyboard (split or curved) | Keeps wrists straight and hands in a natural position, reducing RSI and carpal tunnel risk |
| Vertical or ergonomic mouse; trackball | Holds the hand in a “handshake” position, reducing forearm twisting |
| Wrist rest / palm rest | Supports wrists during pauses (not while typing) |
| Paper stand (document holder) | Holds papers at screen height so you don’t bend your neck |
| Adjustable chair | Adjusts height, backrest and lumbar support |
| Footrest | Supports feet when they cannot reach the floor |
| Monitor stand / monitor arm; laptop stand | Raises the screen to eye level; use with a separate keyboard |
| Headset with microphone | Prevents neck strain from cradling a phone |
## Appropriate lighting
- Use **even, moderate lighting**: offices typically aim for about 300–500 lux for screen work; the room should not be much brighter or darker than the screen.
- Place the screen **at right angles to windows**, not facing or backing onto them, to avoid glare and reflections.
- Use **blinds or curtains** to control sunlight.
- Avoid bright lamps directly behind or in front of the screen; use a **desk lamp** aimed at documents, not the screen.
- Adjust screen brightness to match the room; use dark mode or Night light in dim rooms.

pages.title: Ergonomic Tools and Lighting (continued)
pages.body:
> 🧪 **Activity**
Test the lighting at three computers in the lab: switch lights on and off, open and close curtains, and tilt the screens. Record where glare appears and recommend the best arrangement.

pages.title: Reducing Heat at Workstations
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.1.3.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- discuss heat generated by computers and printers;
- explain how to reduce excess heat.
Electronic components produce **heat** when electricity flows through them. CPUs, graphics cards, power supplies, laser printers (whose fuser rollers reach about 200 °C) and projectors are major heat sources. Many machines in a small room can raise the temperature, causing discomfort, fatigue, equipment failure, data loss and even fire.
| **Measure** | **Why** |
|---|---|
| Good ventilation; air conditioning or fans in labs | Removes hot air and keeps the room comfortable |
| Keep vents clear; leave space behind and around machines | Allows cooling fans to work |
| Clean dust from vents and fans regularly (with power off) | Dust traps heat |
| Do not use laptops on beds, cushions or laps for long periods; use a laptop cooling pad | Soft surfaces block air intake |
| Switch off equipment when not in use; use sleep mode | Less heat and lower electricity bills |
| Keep machines out of direct sunlight | Reduces overheating |
| Place printers and projectors away from people’s seats | Keeps hot air and fumes away from users |
| Monitor temperatures; replace faulty fans | Prevents damage and shutdowns |
